authored_explainer.title: Cereal Output Climbed 1.5x Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s shortage warnings collided with a massive grain boom.
says: Progression to secondary school rose from 77.8% in 1985 to 91.3% by 2017. More students reached the next level.
Cereal production rose from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 million metric tons by 2024. Supply expanded instead of collapsing.
Farmland spans China 5.2, United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, and Russia 2.2 million square kilometers. Food capacity follows land.
authored_explainer.closing: The feared famine missed how quickly education, farming, and supply could improve.
authored_explainer.question: Which food number changes your outlook?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Reached 3.0x Its 1990 Level
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, the fastest-growing energy source wasn't solar or wind.
says: Combustible renewables and waste rose from 10.2% in 1990 to 30.1% in 2024—3.0 times higher. Trash became fuel.
Electricity access climbed from 73.2% in 1998 to 91.9% in 2024—1.3 times higher. Power reached more people.
Waste methane (CH4) rose from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 Mt CO2e in 2024—1.8 times higher. Emissions followed.
authored_explainer.closing: Waste can supply energy, but its growing emissions still affect everyone.
authored_explainer.question: Should waste qualify as renewable?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The population kept growing, but its acceleration nearly disappeared.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025—67 percent of its former share. Humanity shifted toward cities.
Largest-city population barely changed, from 18.2% in 1972 to 16.2% in 2025. Urban growth spread beyond one dominant city.
Population growth slowed from 2% in 1972 to 0.91% in 2025—46 percent of its old pace. The acceleration nearly vanished.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth will reshape schools, housing, workforces, and retirement plans.
authored_explainer.question: Where will slower growth hit first?
